Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BERLIN, Germany (CNN) -- A German cruise liner said Tuesday it plans to fly its passengers over the Gulf of Aden, instead of sailing them through, out of fear of pirate attacks in the region. U.S. Navy image of pirates operating off coast of Somalia in October this year. Hapag-Lloyd Cruises said all 246 passengers and most of the crew aboard the MS Columbus, currently at the start of an around-the-world cruise, will disembark at an undisclosed port, then fly to Dubai to continue their journey. The company called the move a precautionary measure. Pirate attacks in the waters off Somalia have shot up this year, with pirates staging increasingly bolder attacks on ever-bigger targets. So far this year, pirates have attacked almost 100 vessels off Somalia's coast and successfully hijacked nearly 40, according to the International Maritime Bureau. Freight and cargo ships, cruise liners, and private yachts have all come under attack. In many hijackings, pirates take the crew and passengers hostage while they demand a ransom. The problem has forced companies like Hapag-Lloyd, that use the Gulf of Aden, to make new plans, including stepping up security or changing their routes. One shipping company announced last month it would bypass the region altogether, sailing instead around the Cape of Good Hope and adding thousands of kilometers to its voyages. Read more about how to solve the pirate problem here. Hapag-Lloyd said a general travel warning for the area, issued by the German Foreign Ministry, played a part in the decision. But the company also said it had asked the German government for naval protection and the request was turned down. Representatives of Hapag-Lloyd and the German Defense Ministry could not immediately be reached for further comment. The passengers on board the Columbus began the first leg of their world cruise November 28 in Genoa, Italy and are due in Dubai on December 17, according to Hapag-Lloyd's Web site. Further stops include Singapore, Bali, Indonesia and Sydney, Australia. Hapag-Lloyd said that after the passengers and most of the crew disembark, the Columbus will sail through the Gulf of Aden with a skeleton staff. The passengers will stay in a five-star hotel in Dubai for three days until the Columbus arrives to take them back onboard, the company said. Both the crew and passengers approve of the safety measure, Hapag-Lloyd said. The U.S. State Department and British Foreign Office advise those traveling near the Somali coast to use extreme caution because of the recent pirate attacks. Last week, the Australian government issued a similar warning about travel to the region. The advice also urged Australian ships "to apply a robust and layered protective security regime" when traveling through the area. -- CNN's Frederik Pleitgen contributed to this report.

BERLIN, Germany (CNN) — A German cruise operator announced Tuesday that, because of concerns about piracy in the Gulf of Aden, it intends to transport passengers by air over the area rather than carry them through it by ship.

A U.S. Navy image showed pirates operating off Somalia’s coast in October of this year.

Hapag-Lloyd Cruises said the 246 passengers, along with most crew members aboard the MS Columbus, would leave the vessel at an unnamed port. They would then be flown to Dubai, where they would resume their around-the-world trip. The company described the decision as a safety precaution.

Pirate activity in the waters near Somalia has risen sharply this year, with attackers targeting larger vessels and carrying out increasingly aggressive operations. According to the International Maritime Bureau, nearly 100 ships have been attacked off Somalia’s coast so far this year, and close to 40 have been successfully seized.

The attacks have involved freight and cargo vessels, cruise ships and privately owned yachts. In many cases, pirates hold passengers and crew members captive while seeking ransom payments.

The threat has pushed companies that travel through the Gulf of Aden, including Hapag-Lloyd, to revise their plans by increasing security measures or altering routes. Last month, one shipping firm said it would avoid the area completely, sending its vessels around the Cape of Good Hope instead — a detour that adds thousands of kilometers to its journeys.

Hapag-Lloyd said its decision was influenced in part by a general travel warning for the region issued by Germany’s Foreign Ministry. The company also said it had requested naval protection from the German government but that the request had been denied.

Officials from Hapag-Lloyd and Germany’s Defense Ministry were not immediately available for additional comment.

According to Hapag-Lloyd’s website, passengers on the Columbus began the first portion of their world cruise on November 28 in Genoa, Italy, and are scheduled to arrive in Dubai on December 17. Later destinations on the itinerary include Singapore; Bali, Indonesia; and Sydney, Australia.

After the passengers and most crew members leave the ship, Hapag-Lloyd said the Columbus will pass through the Gulf of Aden with only a minimal crew aboard. The passengers are to spend three days at a five-star hotel in Dubai while waiting for the ship to arrive and bring them back onboard, the company said.

Hapag-Lloyd said both passengers and crew members support the safety plan.

The U.S. State Department and Britain’s Foreign Office have advised travelers near Somalia’s coast to exercise extreme caution because of the recent piracy incidents. The Australian government issued a similar warning last week for travel in the region. Its guidance also called on Australian vessels passing through the area “to apply a robust and layered protective security regime.”

CNN’s Frederik Pleitgen contributed to this report.

The cruise line said the precautionary measure was taken as the vessel prepared to transit waters off the coast of Somalia, where piracy has posed a threat to commercial shipping and passenger vessels. Instead of remaining on board for that leg of the voyage, passengers were disembarked and flown to the United Arab Emirates, where they were expected to rejoin the ship after it cleared the high-risk area.

The company described the decision as a safety measure, saying the security of passengers and crew was its highest priority. The ship continued through the region with a reduced number of people on board and additional security precautions in place, according to the operator.

The Gulf of Aden, which connects the Red Sea to the Arabian Sea, is a key route for vessels traveling between Europe and Asia via the Suez Canal. But the narrow corridor has long been vulnerable to attacks by armed pirates operating from Somalia’s coastline. International naval patrols have helped reduce incidents in recent years, though shipping companies continue to treat the area as a security risk.

Cruise operators have occasionally altered routes, canceled stops or added security teams when voyages pass near the Horn of Africa. In some cases, ships travel at higher speeds, keep exterior lights low at night and maintain anti-piracy watches while crossing the region.

Passengers affected by the German cruise line’s decision were provided flights and accommodations as part of the rerouting plan. The company said the broader itinerary would resume once the vessel reached safer waters near Dubai.

Maritime security experts say the move reflects the unusual challenges faced by cruise companies operating in regions where passenger safety must be weighed against maintaining planned schedules.

“Cargo vessels can harden themselves and sail with minimal crew, but cruise ships are different,” one analyst said. “When hundreds of tourists are on board, operators tend to take a much more cautious approach.”

No attack on the ship was reported.

**Hapag-Lloyd to Fly Cruise Passengers as Columbus Crosses Gulf of Aden With Skeleton Crew**

**BERLIN, Dec.  —** German cruise operator Hapag-Lloyd has decided to take passengers off its cruise ship *Columbus* and fly them past one of the world’s most dangerous shipping corridors while the vessel transits the Gulf of Aden with only essential crew on board, the company said.

The move, an unusual precaution for a passenger cruise vessel, reflects growing concern over piracy off Somalia and in the Gulf of Aden, where armed groups have attacked commercial ships, seized vessels and demanded multimillion-dollar ransoms.

Under the plan, passengers aboard the *Columbus* will disembark before the ship enters the high-risk area and travel by air to rejoin the vessel after it has completed the passage. The ship will continue through the Gulf of Aden with a reduced operating crew, minimizing the number of people exposed to any potential attack.

Hapag-Lloyd said the decision was taken as a safety measure and was not based on a specific threat against the vessel. The company said the ship remained seaworthy and would follow established security procedures during the transit.

The *Columbus*, a cruise ship operated by Hapag-Lloyd Cruises, had been scheduled to pass through the Gulf of Aden as part of a longer itinerary linking ports in the Middle East, Asia and Europe. Rather than cancel the voyage outright, the operator opted to separate the passenger portion of the trip from the vessel’s movement through the piracy zone.

Shipping companies have increasingly adopted defensive measures in the region, including rerouting vessels around the Cape of Good Hope, traveling in convoy, increasing speed, posting extra lookouts, using razor wire and water hoses, and coordinating with naval forces deployed in the area.

The Gulf of Aden is a key maritime link between the Indian Ocean and the Red Sea, leading to the Suez Canal. Thousands of vessels use the route each year, including oil tankers, container ships and bulk carriers. But pirate attacks surged in the late 2000s as armed groups operating from Somalia extended their reach farther offshore, often using small boats launched from larger “mother ships.”

Cruise vessels are considered especially sensitive targets because of the large number of civilians on board and the potential political fallout from a hostage situation. Although many pirate attacks have focused on commercial cargo ships, passenger vessels have also been viewed as vulnerable because of their high profile and limited ability to defend themselves.

Hapag-Lloyd’s decision underscores the costs imposed on the shipping and travel industries by Somali piracy. Flying passengers around the danger zone adds logistical complexity and expense, while transiting with a skeleton crew reduces potential casualties but does not eliminate the risk to the vessel or its crew.

International naval patrols from the European Union, NATO, the United States and other countries have been operating in the region to escort vulnerable shipping and deter attacks. Maritime authorities continue to advise vessels to register their movements, maintain a high state of vigilance and avoid predictable routes where possible.

The company said the *Columbus* was expected to resume its normal cruise schedule once the Gulf of Aden transit was complete and passengers had rejoined the ship.
